nodes.label: Mathematical Statements and Logical Connectives
nodes.explanation: Assumes university entry background in elementary algebra (manipulating arithmetic expressions, equations, and inequalities over familiar number systems ℕ, ℤ, ℚ, and ℝ) and informal familiarity with geometric or algebraic justifications. Distinguishes truth-apt mathematical statements (propositions) from algebraic expressions, commands, definitions, and open sentences containing free variables whose truth depends on an assignment. Develops the core propositional connectives—negation (¬), conjunction (∧), and inclusive disjunction (∨)—through exact truth tables, explicitly contrasting mathematical inclusive "or" with everyday exclusive "or" and training unambiguous parenthesization and connective precedence. Uses truth tables to evaluate compound statements and introduces logical equivalence (≡) as identical truth values across all rows, proving basic algebraic laws such as double negation, commutativity, associativity, distributivity, and De Morgan's laws for ¬(P ∧ Q) and ¬(P ∨ Q). Enables the learner to classify mathematical sentences, symbolize everyday mathematical claims using ¬, ∧, and ∨, negate conjunctions and disjunctions accurately, and test equivalence of propositional formulas. Leaves conditionals, biconditionals, quantifiers, and proof writing to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Conditionals, Biconditionals, and Logical Equivalences
nodes.explanation: Builds on statements, basic connectives, and truth-table equivalence to develop the material conditional (P ⇒ Q) and biconditional (P ⇔ Q). Establishes the truth table for P ⇒ Q, confronting the central misconception of vacuous truth (why P ⇒ Q is true whenever P is false, separating logical implication from temporal or causal dependence) and unpacking English phrasings for necessary versus sufficient conditions ("only if", "provided that", "unless"). Distinguishes an implication P ⇒ Q from its converse (Q ⇒ P), inverse (¬P ⇒ ¬Q), and contrapositive (¬Q ⇒ ¬P), proving via truth tables that P ⇒ Q ≡ ¬Q ⇒ ¬P ≡ ¬P ∨ Q while the converse and inverse are equivalent to each other but not to P ⇒ Q. Proves the critical negation law ¬(P ⇒ Q) ≡ P ∧ ¬Q—explicitly targeting the error of negating "if P then Q" as another conditional—and introduces tautologies, contradictions, and algebraic simplification of formulas by substituting established equivalences. Enables the learner to translate "necessary/sufficient" and "if and only if" phrasings accurately, form converses and contrapositives, negate conditionals, and simplify compound statements without rebuilding full truth tables. Leaves rules of deductive inference, quantifiers, and mathematical proofs to later lessons.

nodes.label: Valid Rules of Inference and Propositional Fallacies
nodes.explanation: Builds on conditionals, biconditionals, and tautologies to connect propositional logic to deductive argument structure. Defines validity of an argument (whenever all premises are true, the conclusion must be true, equivalently (P₁ ∧ ··· ∧ P_k) ⇒ C is a tautology) and distinguishes logical validity from soundness (validity plus true premises). Develops the standard propositional inference rules—modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical syllogism, disjunctive syllogism, conjunction, simplification, addition, and proof-by-cases ((P ∨ Q) ∧ (P ⇒ R) ∧ (Q ⇒ R)) ⇒ R—and practices chaining short multi-step propositional deductions. Uses counterassignments (truth-value rows making all premises true and the conclusion false) to refute invalid argument schemas, explicitly diagnosing the classic fallacies of affirming the consequent (converse error), denying the antecedent (inverse error), false dichotomy, and circular reasoning. Enables the learner to verify valid propositional deductions and expose invalid reasoning patterns before working inside mathematical definitions. Leaves quantified inference and writing prose proofs to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Predicates, Domains, and Single Quantifiers
nodes.explanation: Builds on conditionals, biconditionals, and propositional negation to formalize quantified mathematical statements with one quantifier. Introduces predicates (open sentences P(x)) over an explicit domain of discourse—using familiar number systems ℕ, ℤ, ℚ, and ℝ informally without formal set-theoretic machinery—and defines universal quantification (∀x ∈ D, P(x)) and existential quantification (∃x ∈ D, P(x)), showing how changing the domain can flip a statement's truth value. Establishes restricted quantification and explains the crucial pairing convention: universal claims over a condition use ⇒ (∀x ∈ D, P(x) ⇒ Q(x)), whereas existential claims use ∧ (∃x ∈ D, P(x) ∧ Q(x)), diagnosing why writing ∀x (P(x) ∧ Q(x)) or ∃x (P(x) ⇒ Q(x)) distorts meaning (including vacuous truth when P(x) fails for some or all x). Develops negation of single-quantified statements—¬(∀x, P(x)) ≡ ∃x, ¬P(x) and ¬(∃x, P(x)) ≡ ∀x, ¬P(x)—combining these with ¬(P ⇒ Q) ≡ P ∧ ¬Q to negate universal conditionals accurately. Enables the learner to translate quantified mathematical English into symbols and back, determine truth values on concrete domains, and write clean positive negations of single-quantified claims. Leaves multi-quantifier order and proof construction to the next lessons.

nodes.label: Normal Forms and Functional Completeness
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment building on conditionals, biconditionals, and propositional equivalences to analyze canonical representations of Boolean functions. Develops disjunctive normal form (DNF) and conjunctive normal form (CNF) both directly from a formula's truth table (reading minterms from true rows or maxterms from false rows) and algebraically via implication elimination, De Morgan's laws, and distributivity. Defines functional completeness of a set of connectives, proves that {¬, ∧, ∨}, {¬, ∧}, {¬, ∨}, and each of the single connectives NAND (↑) and NOR (↓) are functionally complete by expressing ¬ and ∧ (or ∨) from them, and proves that {∧, ∨} is not functionally complete via the truth-preserving invariant (any formula built from ∧ and ∨ evaluates to true when all atoms are true, so it cannot represent ¬P). Enables the learner to convert propositional formulas into CNF/DNF and prove or refute functional completeness of candidate connective sets, without introducing Boolean algebras or formal axiomatic proof systems.

nodes.label: Nested Quantifiers, Order Dependence, and Uniqueness
nodes.explanation: Builds on predicates and single quantifiers to master statements with two or more quantifiers. Establishes quantifier commutation and non-commutation: adjacent quantifiers of the same type commute (∀x∀y ≡ ∀y∀x, ∃x∃y ≡ ∃y∃x), whereas mixed quantifiers do not—proving (∃y∀x P(x, y)) ⇒ (∀x∃y P(x, y)) while refuting the converse with concrete arithmetic examples (such as "every integer has a larger integer" versus "there is an integer larger than every integer") and framing variable dependence through the Prover–Challenger game (an existential choice may depend only on universally quantified variables to its left). Trains step-by-step negation of nested quantified statements by pushing ¬ past each quantifier and applying conditional/De Morgan rewrites, including multi-quantifier statements modeled on real-analysis syntax (such as boundedness or ε–δ-style inequalities treated purely as logical structure without requiring calculus proofs). Introduces the uniqueness quantifier ∃!x P(x) and its logical unpacking into existence (∃x P(x)) plus uniqueness (∀x∀y, (P(x) ∧ P(y)) ⇒ x = y). Enables the learner to interpret quantifier dependence, judge truth of nested statements, and write accurate idiomatic negations of complex mathematical claims. Leaves proving quantified claims to subsequent proof-method lessons.

nodes.label: Mathematical Definitions and Direct Proof
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes valid propositional inference with predicates and single quantifiers to transition from symbolic logic to writing complete university-level direct proofs. Clarifies the logical role of mathematical definitions (treated as biconditionals even when prose uses "if") and supplies concrete working definitions in elementary arithmetic—even/odd integers, divisibility (a | b meaning ∃k ∈ ℤ with b = ak), rational numbers, and standard ordering/algebra properties of ℤ and ℝ—as accessible proving grounds without requiring formal set theory. Develops the direct proof template for ∀x ∈ D, P(x) ⇒ Q(x): introduce an arbitrary x ∈ D satisfying P(x) (universal generalization from an arbitrary element), unpack definitions with fresh existential variable names, chain valid deductions using algebraic identities and inference rules, and conclude Q(x). Targets critical beginner errors: reusing the same existential witness symbol for two independent objects (writing both even numbers as 2k instead of 2k and 2m), testing numerical examples in place of a general argument, and arguing backward from the conclusion without checking that every step reverses cleanly. Enables the learner to unpack unfamiliar definitions and write clear, logically airtight direct proofs of universal conditional statements. Leaves case splits, contraposition, contradiction, and existence/uniqueness proofs to dedicated follow-up lessons.

nodes.label: Proof by Exhaustive Cases and Symmetry (WLOG)
nodes.explanation: Builds on definitions and direct proof (together with the propositional case-analysis rule established earlier) to handle statements whose hypotheses naturally split into distinct regimes. Develops proof by cases by partitioning the domain or hypothesis into mutually exhaustive possibilities—such as parity (even/odd), sign and absolute-value regimes (x < 0, x = 0, x > 0), and remainder classes modulo 3 or 4 (explicitly supplying the division algorithm on ℤ as an input without proving it)—and proving the target conclusion cleanly in each case, including classic worked uses like the triangle inequality |x + y| ≤ |x| + |y| and parity/divisibility of n(n + 1) or n² − n. Develops disciplined use of "without loss of generality" (WLOG) by requiring an explicit symmetry justification (such as swapping variables a and b when both hypothesis and conclusion are symmetric in a and b, or negating a variable when sign symmetry holds), contrasting valid WLOG reductions with illicit assumptions that omit asymmetric cases. Enables the learner to design exhaustive case splits, audit boundaries like 0 for missing cases, and collapse symmetric cases rigorously. Leaves contraposition, contradiction, and non-constructive excluded-middle arguments to separate lessons.

nodes.label: Proof by Contraposition
nodes.explanation: Builds on definitions and direct proof (and relies on the contrapositive equivalence P ⇒ Q ≡ ¬Q ⇒ ¬P established in earlier ancestors) to prove conditional statements indirectly when a direct route stalls. Trains the exact structure of proof by contraposition for ∀x ∈ D, P(x) ⇒ Q(x): fix an arbitrary x ∈ D, assume ¬Q(x), and derive ¬P(x) directly. Develops structural heuristics for recognizing when contraposition pays off—such as conclusions asserting a negative property or disjunction (where De Morgan's law converts ¬Q into a rich conjunction) or hypotheses involving composite expressions (as in "if n² is even then n is even", "if ab is even then a is even or b is even", or "if x + y is irrational then x is irrational or y is irrational"). Explicitly contrasts contraposition with the converse error (proving Q ⇒ P instead of ¬Q ⇒ ¬P) and flags how negation interacts with quantified conclusions or compound hypotheses. Enables the learner to convert conditional statements accurately to their contrapositives, choose contraposition strategically, and execute clean contrapositive proofs. Leaves proof by contradiction and biconditional/equivalence-chain proofs to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Existence Proofs, Uniqueness Proofs, and Counterexamples
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes nested quantifiers (including variable dependence and ∃!) with definitions and direct proof to prove existential and uniqueness claims and to refute false conjectures. Develops constructive existence proofs for ∃x P(x) (exhibiting a concrete witness and verifying both domain membership and P(x)) and for ∀x∃y P(x, y) (constructing y explicitly in terms of an arbitrary x, checking that y obeys quantifier dependence and never lets an outer existential depend on an inner universal). Develops uniqueness proofs via the standard two-element template (assume P(x₁) and P(x₂) and deduce x₁ = x₂) or by showing any solution must equal a specific formula, combining existence and uniqueness to prove ∃! statements (such as unique linear solutions or unique representation under constraints). Trains rigorous disproof: refuting ∀x P(x) or ∀x (P(x) ⇒ Q(x)) by exhibiting a single verified counterexample satisfying P(x) ∧ ¬Q(x), contrasted with disproving an existential claim ∃x P(x) (which requires proving the universal statement ∀x ¬P(x)) and disproving nested statements like ∃y∀x P(x, y) (which requires proving ∀y∃x ¬P(x, y)). Enables the learner to construct witnesses, prove uniqueness, and decisively disprove false statements while avoiding the misconception that examples prove universal claims. Leaves non-constructive existence proofs to an optional enrichment lesson.

nodes.label: Proof by Contradiction
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes nested quantifier negation with definitions and direct proof to develop proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum). Establishes the logical schema—proving S by assuming ¬S and deducing an explicit contradiction R ∧ ¬R, and specifically proving P ⇒ Q by assuming P ∧ ¬Q rather than ¬P ⇒ ¬Q—and applies it to non-conditional, negative, and quantified claims where neither direct proof nor contraposition applies naturally. Develops canonical university proofs: irrationality of √2 (explicitly supplying that every rational number can be written in lowest terms a/b with a, b ∈ ℤ not both even, without requiring induction or full number theory), nonexistence of a smallest positive rational number, and Euclid's proof of the infinitude of primes (explicitly supplying that every integer greater than 1 has a prime divisor). Trains crucial proof hygiene: identifying the exact contradiction reached, avoiding "disguised contraposition" (where assuming P ∧ ¬Q only derives ¬P and a direct contrapositive proof would be cleaner), and diagnosing false contradictions produced by introducing an unjustified extra assumption. Enables the learner to set up ¬S cleanly for quantified and conditional statements and execute valid contradiction proofs. Leaves mathematical induction and well-ordering arguments to separate modules.

nodes.label: Biconditional Proofs and Equivalence Chains (TFAE)
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes proof by contraposition and proof by contradiction (alongside direct proof from earlier ancestors) to prove biconditional theorems P ⇔ Q and multi-statement equivalences ("the following are equivalent", TFAE). Develops the standard two-direction proof structure—proving P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P separately, often mixing a direct proof for one direction with contraposition or contradiction for the other—and distinguishes it from single-chain "if and only if" algebraic derivations, diagnosing irreversible steps (such as squaring both sides or multiplying by a potentially zero expression) that secretly prove only one direction. Introduces cyclic implication strategies for proving k statements equivalent (e.g., (1) ⇒ (2) ⇒ (3) ⇒ (1) or (1) ⇒ (2) ⇒ (3) ⇒ (4) ⇒ (1)), explaining why any strongly connected directed cycle of k implications establishes all k(k − 1) pairwise implications and training strategic ordering of the cycle to minimize proof difficulty. Applies these tools to concrete arithmetic and inequality characterizations (such as parity/divisibility equivalences and algebraic criteria). Enables the learner to plan and write complete biconditional and TFAE proofs without missing directions or introducing hidden non-equivalences.

nodes.label: Non-Constructive Existence Proofs
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment synthesizing proof by cases, existence proofs, and proof by contradiction to examine pure existence arguments that establish ∃x P(x) without identifying a single explicit witness. Contrasts constructive witness proofs with two classical non-constructive patterns: case splits via the law of excluded middle (exemplified by proving there exist irrational numbers a and b such that a^b is rational by analyzing (√2)^√2 and ((√2)^√2)^√2, without deciding which case actually holds) and indirect existence by contradiction (such as proving there are infinitely many primes of the form 4k + 3 using the product 4(p₁ ··· p_r) − 1 and parity/remainder analysis modulo 4, supplying prime factorization of integers > 1 as an input). Clarifies why such arguments are fully valid in classical mathematics while noting what extra information a constructive proof provides. Enables the learner to follow and construct elementary non-constructive existence arguments, without introducing the Axiom of Choice, Zorn's Lemma, or mathematical induction.

nodes.label: Proof Strategy Selection and Proof Auditing
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes proof by cases, existence/uniqueness/counterexamples, and biconditional/equivalence-chain proofs (with contraposition, contradiction, and nested quantifiers available through its prerequisites) to develop independent mathematical problem-solving and proof-verification judgment. Trains a systematic workflow for unlabeled conjectures: test small and edge cases first to form a hypothesis about truth or falsity, then match the claim's outer logical structure and definitions to the cleanest proof method (direct, cases, contraposition, contradiction, constructive witness, counterexample, or cyclic equivalence) rather than defaulting mechanically to contradiction. Trains line-by-line proof auditing on realistic flawed proofs containing subtle defects—circularity (assuming the conclusion), converse/inverse errors, illegal division by zero, unverified existential instantiation or witness reuse, reversed quantifier dependence, incomplete case splits, and faulty negation of nested quantifiers—requiring the learner not only to spot the broken step but to determine whether the underlying theorem is salvageable or false. Enables the learner to evaluate novel mathematical claims independently, select and execute an appropriate proof or disproof, and critique proofs with precision. Leaves formal set theory, mappings, and mathematical induction to subsequent courses.
